title: Transaction Concept
description: Define a database transaction from business invariants, trace commit and rollback boundaries, and distinguish statement success, resource scope and uncertain outcomes.

questions.question_text: What is a transaction?
options: A single SQL keyword
A sequence of operations treated as a single, indivisible logical unit of work
A synonym for a database table
A type of index
questions.explanation: A transaction bundles operations so they succeed or fail together.

questions.question_text: Why should both required supported debit and credit writes belong to the same correctly handled transaction?
options: To make the two statements run faster
So money can never leave one account without arriving at the other, even if something fails partway through
Because SQL requires exactly two statements per transaction
To avoid needing a WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Grouping supports one database commit outcome; the workflow must still verify both required effects, authorization and sufficient source state.

questions.question_text: With MySQL autocommit enabled and no explicit transaction active, is a successful standalone InnoDB INSERT ordinarily a transaction?
options: No, only multi-statement blocks are transactions
Yes, the successful standalone statement completes its own transaction
Only if it inserts two rows
Only after a manual ROLLBACK
questions.explanation: Scope the statement to a successful standalone transactional DML operation outside an explicit transaction.

questions.question_text: Does the database automatically figure out which operations should be grouped into one transaction?
options: Yes, it infers this from the schema
No — this is a business/application design decision; the database only enforces guarantees for whatever you explicitly group
Only for foreign-key-related operations
The database groups every statement in a session automatically
questions.explanation: Transaction boundaries must be deliberately chosen by whoever writes the application logic.

questions.question_text: Will transaction support automatically infer and group a related update the developer omitted from the intended boundary?
options: Yes, it always detects missing related operations
No — this is a design error the database has no way to catch, since it only knows about statements you actually group together
Only if foreign keys are involved
The database automatically adds the missing statement
questions.explanation: The engine enforces declared statements and constraints; a separate constraint might catch a violation, but transaction support does not infer the missing intended grouping.

questions.question_text: Do a transaction's correctness guarantees depend on how many statements it contains?
options: Yes, guarantees only apply to exactly two-statement transactions
No — the guarantees apply regardless of statement count, though very long transactions have separate practical costs
Guarantees only apply to single-statement transactions
Transactions with more than 5 statements are not supported
questions.explanation: Atomicity/consistency guarantees are independent of transaction size, though performance considerations (22.13) are a separate concern.

questions.question_text: Which information is essential when defining a business transaction?
options: Only the source file name
Its participating operations, invariants and actual commit/rollback boundary
Only the number of SQL comments
Only the client screen color
questions.explanation: The operation must identify what succeeds together and how required effects are enforced, rather than rely on course-history trivia.

questions.question_text: What does 'all-or-nothing' mean for a transaction's real-world effect?
options: Every external effect is automatically reversible
The transaction’s supported changes commit as one unit, or its supported pending work is undone when aborted
Every statement error necessarily aborts the whole transaction
All data values become correct automatically
questions.explanation: Statement-scope errors and external effects need separate handling; all-or-nothing concerns the supported transaction outcome.

questions.question_text: What establishes the actual database transaction boundary?
options: Commands or driver operations on the executing connection
A function name alone
An editor tab
A page submission by itself
questions.explanation: Application grouping must correspond to real connection-level transaction control.

questions.question_text: Can a zero-row UPDATE complete without achieving the business request?
options: No, every UPDATE changes a row
Yes
Only for text columns
Only without a WHERE
questions.explanation: Statement success does not establish required entity existence or effects.

questions.question_text: What are the pending quantities after the stated three-kit movement?
options: 12 and 8
9 and 11
9 and 8
12 and 11
questions.explanation: Subtracting and adding three preserves the combined twenty.

questions.question_text: What are the quantities after the stated full rollback?
options: 9 and 11
12 and 11
12 and 8
9 and 8
questions.explanation: Supported pending changes are undone.

questions.question_text: Does an atomic debit 3 and credit 4 preserve the intended total?
options: Yes, atomicity repairs arithmetic
Only with primary keys
Only if committed
No
questions.explanation: Correct business consistency requires the right invariant and logic.

questions.question_text: Does START TRANSACTION automatically include an external email in rollback?
options: No
Yes, all function effects join
Only if sent before COMMIT
Only if the message is short
questions.explanation: External effects require their own coordination contract.

questions.question_text: Why must the owner inspect error scope?
options: Every error is identical
Some failures undo one statement while others abort the transaction
Every exception commits
Every failure disables checks
questions.explanation: Cleanup must match the actual remaining transaction state.

questions.question_text: Can an explicit transaction coexist with autocommit setting 1?
options: No
Only on a replica
Yes
Only for empty tables
questions.explanation: The mode governs default standalone statements outside the explicit unit.

questions.question_text: What should precede retry after a lost commit response?
options: Blind repetition of all effects
A new random identity every time
An unsupported success claim
Authorized reconciliation of the request outcome
questions.explanation: The server may already have committed the operation.

questions.question_text: Why is reducing duration by committing the debit first unacceptable here?
options: It breaks the required grouped movement boundary
It changes the table name
It prevents every SELECT
It proves stronger isolation
questions.explanation: Performance work must preserve the business invariant.

questions.question_text: Does a one-session arithmetic result prove concurrent safety?
options: Yes, all engines are identical
No
Only if sorted
Only with two rows
questions.explanation: Controlled sessions and actual interleavings are separate evidence.

questions.question_text: What must a pooled connection not carry into another request?
options: A documented stable identifier
A confirmed completed outcome
Unresolved transactional work
An approved query template
questions.explanation: Pending state can leak locks and effects across unrelated borrowers.

original_questions.question_text: Where was the transaction concept first introduced practically in this course?
options: Chapter 20 (Indexes)
Chapter 8 (TCL) and Chapter 11 (Data Modification Transactions)
Chapter 1 (Database Foundations)
Chapter 16 (Joins)
original_questions.explanation: This chapter builds on the practical TCL introduction from earlier chapters.

original_questions.question_text: What does 'all-or-nothing' mean for a transaction's real-world effect?
options: At least half the statements must succeed
Either every statement's effect becomes permanent, or none of them do
The first statement always succeeds regardless of the rest
Statements are applied in random order
original_questions.explanation: This is the essence of atomicity — no partial completion is a valid outcome.

notes:
## Define the business operation before its SQL boundary

A database transaction is a unit of work whose participating operations share a defined completion decision. It can read data, modify data or do both. The application chooses which related operations must succeed together, while the database supplies its supported transaction mechanisms. A screen submission, source file or function call does not automatically correspond to one database transaction. Identify the actual begin, commit and rollback boundaries on the connection doing the work.

Imagine moving three workshop kits from one depot to another. The source quantity decreases by three and the destination increases by three. The business operation also requires both depots to exist, enough source stock and an authorized actor. Grouping the updates in one transaction supports an all-or-nothing database outcome, but it does not invent those missing requirements. A reliable design names the invariant and the trusted checks as well as the SQL commands.

## Separate a complete effect from individual statement success

An UPDATE can complete successfully while matching no row. If the source depot exists but the destination does not, the debit can change a row and the credit can do nothing without necessarily producing an error. Committing that transaction can be atomic at the database level while failing the intended kit movement. Statement success must therefore be distinguished from required business effects.

Use a disposable InnoDB fixture with two known depots to study the boundary. The example deliberately rolls back so its pending changes can be compared with the original committed rows. Build the table and seed outside the demonstration transaction, because ordinary DDL can introduce separate commit behavior in MySQL. Keep the quantities small enough to verify every row manually.

```sql
CREATE TABLE kit_stock (
  depot_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>=0)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO kit_stock VALUES(1,12),(2,8);
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE kit_stock SET quantity=quantity-3
WHERE depot_id=1 AND quantity>=3;
-- Trusted workflow verifies the required source effect.
UPDATE kit_stock SET quantity=quantity+3 WHERE depot_id=2;
-- Trusted workflow verifies destination and request invariants.
SELECT depot_id,quantity FROM kit_stock ORDER BY depot_id;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT depot_id,quantity FROM kit_stock ORDER BY depot_id;
```

The first ordered result is nine and eleven, observed by the writing transaction before completion. After rollback the result is twelve and eight. A successful business path would commit only after its required conditions were established. The comments identify checks that the application must implement; they are not executable guards and must not be mistaken for a complete production stock-transfer procedure.

## Connect transaction properties to distinct questions

Atomicity concerns the supported unit's commit outcome: participating pending work does not remain as a partially committed transaction after abort. Consistency concerns preserving the specified valid-state invariants through correct logic and enforcement. Isolation concerns concurrent interactions and observations under the chosen contract. Durability concerns survival of committed work within documented persistence settings and failure assumptions.

These properties support reliable operations but do not repair arbitrary application mistakes. Subtracting three and adding four can be atomic while violating conservation. An unauthorized request can be durable. A weak isolation mode can permit anomalies even though the engine supports transactions. State which property addresses each failure scenario rather than treating the acronym as one universal proof of correctness.

## Understand one-statement and multi-statement transactions

With MySQL autocommit enabled and no explicit transaction active, a successful standalone transactional DML statement normally completes its own transaction. Two such UPDATE statements do not automatically form one atomic kit movement. If the process fails after the first commits, a later ROLLBACK cannot undo that already completed transaction. Code proximity does not join the boundaries.

START TRANSACTION can establish an explicit boundary while the session autocommit setting remains enabled. COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends that explicit unit, and subsequent standalone work follows the session behavior again. Drivers and frameworks can control these boundaries through APIs, so inspect their documented behavior rather than assuming an editor's displayed sequence matches the server's execution context.

A transaction does not need many statements to be meaningful. A single conditional decrement can be a complete supported unit for a narrowly defined counter operation. Conversely, many statements can belong to one business unit when the invariant spans several rows. Statement count affects practical duration and resource use, but it does not define which changes must succeed together.

## Include reads and decisions in the concurrency design

Reading quantity in one statement, calculating a replacement in application memory and writing it later can race with another request. Two requests can both read twelve and independently decide that three kits are available. Appropriate conditional relative updates, locking reads or another verified concurrency strategy must connect the decision with the change. Merely wrapping arbitrary stale-value assignments between transaction keywords is not a complete concurrency argument.

For a multirow invariant, identify every row and predicate the decision depends on. Locking only the source can be insufficient for a rule also involving destination capacity or a shared aggregate. A serializable strategy may require retries; a consistent lock order can reduce certain deadlock patterns. Test the actual permitted, denied and failed histories rather than selecting a mechanism solely because its name sounds strongest.

## Keep all participants within the stated resource scope

InnoDB row changes participate in transactional rollback, while nontransactional table writes do not acquire equivalent support because START TRANSACTION appears nearby. Ordinary DDL can cause implicit commits, and temporary-table operations have their own exceptions. Verify storage engines and statement semantics before promising that one rollback can reverse an entire script.

An email, remote charge or unrelated file write is also outside ordinary database rollback. An outbox can record notification intent with the database change and deliver it later under a reviewed protocol, but delivery introduces its own retry and duplicate-handling responsibilities. A transaction boundary is useful only when its participants are stated honestly; it cannot silently extend across every external action in an application function.

## Handle failure scope and uncertain completion

Some InnoDB errors roll back only the failing statement while earlier successful work remains pending. Deadlock handling can roll back the complete transaction. The trusted owner must use documented error scope, decide whether the whole business attempt failed and explicitly resolve it. Returning a pooled connection with an open transaction can leak locks and pending work into an unrelated later request.

A connection can disappear after a server commits but before the response reaches the caller. The client then has an unknown outcome. Do not equate the network failure with confirmed rollback or repeat a stock movement blindly. Reconciliation using a stable authorized request identity can determine whether the intended effect already completed. Verify ownership and payload meaning before treating an existing identifier as an equivalent successful request.

## Keep transactions short without breaking the invariant

Long transactions can retain locks, snapshots and recovery-related resources. Avoid user interaction and slow unrelated network calls inside a protected interval. However, shortening the transaction by committing the debit before the credit simply abandons the original all-or-nothing requirement. Optimize the work and access paths while preserving the boundary the business operation needs.

Separate fixture setup, explanatory inspection and operational commands in a teaching lab. Reset the starting rows between experiments so an earlier committed movement does not masquerade as a failed rollback. Record exact connection identities, outcomes and engine versions when executing examples. A successful one-session arithmetic run is narrower evidence than controlled concurrency, crash recovery or hosted-provider verification.

## Solve two boundary exercises

First exercise: run the stated rollback history from twelve and eight. The pending result is nine and eleven; the final result returns to twelve and eight. Replace rollback with a correctly checked commit and describe why the intended final movement remains. Then remove the destination in a new fixture and explain why a zero-row credit requires the trusted workflow's failure path.

Second exercise: compare two independently autocommitted updates with one explicit transaction when a failure occurs between the debit and credit. The first can leave the source changed alone; the second can discard its supported pending debit through a confirmed full rollback. Continue with [ACID](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/acid), [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries) and [atomicity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/atomicity) to connect the logical operation to each supported guarantee.

diagrams.caption: A logical kit movement needs a complete trusted boundary
diagrams.description: A source debit and destination credit remain pending together, then the trusted owner chooses commit or rollback after required checks. External effects do not automatically participate.
